title: Interview: Ravi Kumar — Senior Frontend Engineer
segments: Hi Ravi, welcome. I'm Alex, I lead product engineering, and Jenna is a senior engineer on our frontend team. We'll spend about forty minutes on your background, a system design discussion and your questions.
Thanks, great to meet you both. I'm excited to be here.
To start, could you tell us about a recent frontend project you're proud of?

Sure. At my current company I led the rebuild of our analytics dashboard. The old version rendered every chart on load, and it took eight seconds to become interactive. I moved us to server components for the shell, virtualized the large tables, and lazy loaded charts as they scrolled into view. Time to interactive dropped to under two seconds.
Nice. How did you decide what to render on the server versus the client?

Anything static or user-independent went to the server, like layout, navigation and saved report metadata. Interactive pieces with local state, like filters and the chart tooltips, stayed on the client. We measured each change with real user monitoring so we weren't guessing.
How did you bring the rest of the team along on that change?
I wrote a short RFC, ran a lunch-and-learn on virtualization, and paired with two engineers on the first migrations. After that, the team migrated the remaining pages themselves.

Let's move to a design question. Imagine you're building the transcript view for a meeting app. The transcript can be three hours long, with thousands of segments, and it has to stay in sync with an audio player. How would you approach it?

First, I'd keep a single source of truth for the current playback time, probably a context or small store that the player writes to. The transcript reads from it to figure out which segment is active, using a binary search over the start times, because a linear scan on every time update would be wasteful.

I'd virtualize the list so only the visible segments plus a buffer are in the DOM. The tricky part is auto-scrolling to the active segment. With virtualization you scroll by index rather than by element ref. I'd also pause auto-scroll when the user scrolls manually and show a button to resume, otherwise it fights the user.
What about search within the transcript?

I'd compute matches on the full transcript data rather than the DOM, store the match positions, and highlight them when segments render. Next and previous buttons would scroll to the segment index of each match. For very long transcripts, I'd debounce the input and maybe do the matching in a web worker.
Good. How would you test the sync behavior?

I'd unit test the active-segment lookup with edge cases like gaps between segments and seeking past the end. Then I'd add a component test with a fake media element where I control the current time, and one end-to-end test that clicks a segment and checks the player time.
Really solid. We have about ten minutes left. What questions do you have for us?
How does the frontend team decide what to work on, and how much ownership do engineers have over the roadmap?
Engineers co-write the quarterly roadmap with product. Each sprint has a clear goal, and engineers usually own a feature end to end, from design review to release.
That's great. And what does success look like in the first ninety days for this role?
Shipping one meaningful improvement to the meeting page, and leading the performance work for long transcripts. Honestly, it's very close to the problem we just discussed.
That sounds like exactly the kind of work I enjoy. Thank you both.
Thank you, Ravi. Our recruiter will be in touch within a few days about next steps.

summary.overview: Ravi Kumar interviewed for the Senior Frontend Engineer role. He described rebuilding an analytics dashboard with server components, table virtualization and lazy-loaded charts, which cut time to interactive from 8s to under 2s, and how he brought the team along with an RFC and pairing. In the system design exercise on a long, audio-synced transcript, he proposed a single playback-time store, binary search for the active segment, a virtualized list, pausable auto-scroll, and search over data rather than the DOM, along with a sensible testing plan. Strong signal on performance and on communication.
